blocks.title: Photoelectric effect
blocks.text: The process of emission of electrons from a metal surface when exposed to light of suitable frequency or wavelength is called the photoelectric effect. The emitted electrons are known as photoelectrons.

The photoelectric effect is demonstrated by the apparatus shown in Fig. 18.1. An evacuated glass tube X contains two electrodes. The electrode B connected to the positive terminal of the battery acts as anode. The metal electrode C connected to negative terminal acts as cathode. When monochromatic light of suitable frequency is allowed to shine on cathode, it begins to emit electrons. These photoelectrons are attracted by the positive anode and the resulting current is measured by a micro-ammeter. The current stops when light is cut off, which proves that the current flows because of incident light. This current is, hence, called photoelectric current.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book calls the anode 'electrode B' here; Fig. 18.1 and the next paragraph label it A (anode A).

blocks.alt: Incident light passes through a colour filter onto the photocell X, which holds the cathode C and the anode A. A micro-ammeter A is in series with the cell, a voltmeter V is connected across it, and the cell is fed from the sliding contact of the potential divider Y, which is connected to a battery.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.1: Experimental arrangement to observe photoelectric effect (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.1).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the printed Figure 18.1 the photocell's right-hand wire is not joined to the potential divider, which leaves the circuit open. It is joined to the end of the divider, as drawn above.

The maximum energy of the photoelectrons can be determined by reversing the connections of the battery in the circuit i.e., now the anode A is negative and cathode C is at positive potential. In this condition, the photoelectrons are repelled by the anode and the photoelectric current decreases. If this potential is made more and more negative, at a certain value, called stopping potential V₀, the current becomes zero. If the experiment is repeated with light beam of higher intensity, the amount of current increases but the current stops for the same value of V₀. blocks.text: However, if the intensity is kept constant and experiment is performed with different frequencies of incident light, we obtain the curves as shown in Fig.18.3. The current is same but stopping potential is different for each frequency of incident light, which indicates the proportionality of maximum kinetic energy with frequency of light f.

blocks.caption: Figure 18.3: Characteristic curves of photocurrent vs applied voltage for light of different frequencies (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.3).

blocks.text: The important results as indicated by the graph between (K.E.)max and frequency of incident light of the experiments are:

items: The electrons are emitted with different energies. The maximum energy of photoelectrons depends on the particular metal surface and the frequency of incident light.

There is a minimum frequency called threshold frequency below which no electrons are emitted, however, intense the light may be. For example, blue light produces photoelectric emission in sodium metal but red light does not (Fig. 18.4). This threshold frequency f₀ varies from metal to metal. The corresponding wavelength of incident light is called threshold wavelength.
Electrons are emitted instantaneously; the intensity of light determines only their number.

blocks.alt: Two wavy light rays. A red ray with a long wavelength, labelled red light (low intensity), ends at 'No electron emitted'. A blue ray with a short wavelength, labelled blue light (high intensity), ends at 'Electron emitted (more electrons)'.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.4: Red and blue light incident on sodium metal (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.4).

blocks.text: These results could not be explained on the basis of electromagnetic wave theory of light. According to this theory, increasing the intensity of incident light should increase the K.E. of emitted electrons which contradicts the experimental result. The classical theory cannot also explain the threshold frequency of light.
According to this theory, even the light of lesser energy should eventually transfer enough energy to liberate electrons. But this does not happen.
Explanation on the Basis of Quantum Theory

Einstein extended the idea of quantization of energy proposed by Max Planck that light is emitted or absorbed in quanta, a tiny packets of energy, known as photons. The energy of each photon of frequency f as given by quantum theory is:

A photon could be absorbed by a single electron in the metal surface. The electron needs a certain minimum energy called the work function φ to escape from the metal surface. If the energy of incident photon is sufficient, the electron is ejected instantaneously from the metal surface. A part of the photon energy is used by the electron to break away from the metal and the rest appears as the kinetic energy of the electron. That is;

blocks.text_alt: Incident photon energy − Work function = (K.E.)max of photoelectron

blocks.text: This is known as Einstein's photoelectric equation.

It is to be noted that all the emitted electrons do not possess the maximum kinetic energy, some electrons come straight out of the metal surface and some lose energy in atomic collisions before coming out. Equation 18.7 holds good only for those electrons which come out with full surplus energy.
Albert Einstein was awarded Nobel Prize in physics in 1921 for his explanation of photoelectric effect.

The phenomenon of photoelectric effect cannot be explained if we assume that light consists of waves and energy is uniformly distributed over its wavefront. It can only be explained by assuming light consists of small packet of energy known as photons. Thus, it shows the particle nature of light.

blocks.title: Example 18.1
blocks.problem: Find the energy of a photon in eV of the blue light of wavelength 450 nm.
steps:
Wavelength λ = 450 nm = 450 × 10⁻⁹ m
h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Example 18.1 prints 'As 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J × 1 eV'; the relation is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 1 eV (so 1 J = 1/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) eV). The answer 2.76 eV is right.

blocks.problem:

blocks.title: For your information
blocks.text:
Interaction of electromagnetic radiation with matter
(i) At low energies (less than 0.5 MeV), the dominant process is photoelectric effect.
(ii) At intermediate energies, the dominant process is Compton effect.
(iii) At higher energies (more than 1.2MeV), the dominant process is pair production.
